sense: the pull that makes things fall

terms.gloss: weight, heaviness: the tendency of heavy things to fall; gravity
evidence: Cic. N. D. 2.116: tanta contentiō gravitātis et ponderum
Lucr. 2.84: aut gravitāte suā ferrī prīmōrdia rērum
terms.comment: Classically the weight or heaviness of a body, by which it is carried downward or toward the middle of the world (Cicero, Lucretius); the physicist’s force of gravity is a modern sense of it, ours and Egger’s (Morgan–Owens).

terms.gloss: the downward pull of a body, its tendency to fall
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.40: terrēna et ūmida suopte nūtū et suō pondere … in terram et in mare ferantur
Cic. de Or. 3.178: terra … suā vī nūtūque teneātur
terms.comment: Properly a nod; in Cicero, the way a heavy thing “nods” downward of itself (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Cūr mālum dēcidit? Gravitāte suā deorsum fertur.
phrases.english: Why did the apple fall? Gravity pulls it down.

phrases.latin: terrēna et ūmida suopte nūtū et suō pondere ad parīs angulōs in terram et in mare ferantur
phrases.english: that earthy and watery things are carried by their own pull and their own weight straight down to the earth and the sea

phrases.latin: nam quoniam per ināne vagantur, cūncta necessest aut gravitāte suā ferrī prīmōrdia rērum aut ictū forte alterius
phrases.english: for since they wander through the void, the first beginnings of things must all be carried along either by their own weight or by a chance blow from another

sources: Lewis & Short: gravitas · Lewis & Short: nutus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. gravity (physics).
